branch_provenance.syndrome: Acute Episode of Altered Mental Status with Abdominal Pain and Vomiting

state.case_summary:
An 8‐year‐old boy with no significant past medical history presented with a 30-minute history of generalized abdominal pain followed by a single episode of vomiting. During the event he developed diaphoresis, mucocutaneous paleness, dizziness, dysarthria, incoherent speech, and lack of eye contact, without loss of consciousness, abnormal movements, or sphincter relaxation. The episode lasted 10 minutes, after which he reported a frontal headache (5/10) and persistent nausea. Family denied toxin or medication exposure. He had a similar episode 18 months earlier, diagnosed as migraine. There was no personal or family history of epilepsy or neurological disorders. Developmental milestones were age‐appropriate, and he was performing well in school.

On admission, his vital signs were normal except for blood pressure above the 95th percentile for age. Neurologic examination revealed confusion and disorientation; he could not recognize his mother or speak but could follow visual commands. Motor and sensory examinations were normal. Approximately 20 minutes after arrival, his consciousness and orientation improved. Over the next hours he had three additional self‐limited vomiting episodes and ongoing headache, which improved after a single IV dose of diclofenac (1 mg/kg).

Complete blood count, serum chemistries, and electrolytes (including sodium, chloride, potassium, magnesium, and phosphorus) were all within normal limits. Brain MRI with an epilepsy protocol was reported as normal for age.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Self-limited epilepsy with autonomic seizures
B. migraine
C. Migraine was considered because of recurrent headaches with vomiting and a prior similar diagnosis
D. Cyclic vomiting syndrome was considered due to recurrent emetic episodes but was excluded by the absence of metabolic
E. Gastroenteritis was considered because of abdominal pain and vomiting but was unlikely given normal laboratory studies
F. Gastroesophageal reflux disease was considered in the differential for vomiting but was not supported by clinical
G. Syncope was considered because of transient unresponsiveness and pallor but was less likely as he retained the ability
H. None

excluded_candidates: Migraine: possible given past diagnosis, but episode characteristics are atypical
Epilepsy: unlikely given no personal or family history and normal brain MRI
Infectious cause: possible, but no clear evidence of infection
